rfm_tuples.R: 'As of December 31, 2024, we were not in compliance with a debt covenant on one mortgage loan which resulted in an event of default. The Company cured the initial default in October 2024 by depositing $2.7 million in an interest-bearing escrow account held by the lender and deposited an additional $0.8 million in February 2025.' (10-K, Debt Covenants section)
rfm_tuples.f: claim_evolution between prior 10-K (FY23 filed Feb 2024) and current 10-K (FY24 filed Feb 2025) — did the framing of the same covenant issue change?
rfm_tuples.M_value: FY23 10-K (Feb 2024) described the same mortgage covenant non-compliance as 'due to disruption from a significant renovation' and explicitly stated 'This did not result in an event of default' with a 'lender waiver until March 31, 2024.' FY24 10-K now characterizes the SAME mortgage covenant issue as 'an event of default' requiring escrow cure deposits ($2.7M Oct 2024 + $0.8M Feb 2025). Q1 2025 10-Q discloses an additional $1.5M+ deposit bringing total to $5.0M trapped. The framing thus drifted from 'no event of default + waiver' (FY23) to 'event of default + multi-tranche cure' (FY24/Q1'25).
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Same loan, same root cause (renovation/property cash flow shortfall) but the disclosure was upgraded from 'waiver, no default' to 'event of default — cured.' This is real claim drift indicating the issue persisted longer and escalated beyond initial scope. Not a SHORT-tier red flag (REIT total debt is $1.3B; trapped $5M is immaterial; remaining mortgages and the unsecured credit facility are in compliance), but it is concrete forensic evidence of a deteriorating credit narrative rather than the 'transitory renovation disruption' previously implied.

rfm_tuples.R: 'As of December 31, 2024, we were in compliance with all other debt covenants, current on all loan payments and not otherwise in default under the revolving credit facility, corporate credit facility term loans, remaining mortgage loans or Senior Notes.' (10-K, Debt Covenants)
rfm_tuples.f: Cross-check with Q1 2025 10-Q for covenant status drift
rfm_tuples.M_value: Q1 2025 10-Q confirms covenant compliance on all other facilities and provides further detail: 'As of March 31, 2025, the Company was in violation of a debt covenant on one mortgage loan. The Company cured the violation by depositing a total of $5.0 million, inclusive of $3.5 million funded in 2024, in an interest-bearing escrow account held by the lender.' Senior notes, $500M revolver (with $0 drawn after Jan 2025 paydown), and term loans all in compliance.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Claim verified across two consecutive periodic reports. Only the one renovation-affected mortgage loan is in trouble; the unsecured credit complex (where covenants would actually threaten the enterprise) is clean.

rfm_tuples.R: 'We completed most components of the transformative renovation of the former Hyatt Regency Scottsdale Resort & Spa at Gainey Ranch. In November 2024, the property was upbranded to Grand Hyatt Scottsdale Resort.' (10-K, Item 1 Business). Excluding this property, FY24 rooms revenues grew 3.7%; including it, growth was only 1.5%.
rfm_tuples.f: Verify project completion via Q1 2025 10-Q (was the renovation actually mostly complete, or did the company quietly extend the disruption window?)
rfm_tuples.M_value: Q1 2025 10-Q corroborates that 'Grand Hyatt Scottsdale Resort... was undergoing a transformative renovation during 2024' (past tense) and adds: 'In February 2025, we added five newly created rooms at Grand Hyatt Scottsdale Resort.' Excluding the property, Q1 portfolio RevPAR was +4.1%; including it was +6.7% — meaning Scottsdale was actually accretive in Q1'25, consistent with a completed/ramping property.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: The 'renovation complete' claim is verified by both rooms-added disclosure and the reversal of Scottsdale's portfolio drag in Q1 2025 (from -2.2pp drag in FY24 to +2.6pp uplift in Q1'25). No claim drift here.

rfm_tuples.R: 'Approximately 81.1% of our rooms operating under Marriott or Hyatt brands. ... approximately 23%, 20%, and 12% of total rooms were located in Texas, California and Florida, respectively. ... over 30% of the Company's total revenues for the years ended December 31, 2024, 2023 and 2022, respectively, were concentrated in its five largest hotels.' (10-K, Risk Factors + Notes Risks and Uncertainties)
rfm_tuples.f: MODE-B: For a 31-property REIT, top-5-hotel >30% revenue concentration + 81% rooms in two brand families + 55% rooms in three states is a structural concentration risk. Was it disclosed clearly and quantitatively?
rfm_tuples.M_value: Concentration is disclosed in three places: brand affiliation table (Marriott=45%, Hyatt=36% by rooms), geographic table (TX 23% / CA 20% / FL 12%), and explicit '>30% revenues from top 5 hotels' statement in Risks and Uncertainties. Plus 10%+ revenue concentration in Orlando, FL and Houston, TX markets (year-specific markets shifted: 2023 disclosure was Orlando+Phoenix, 2022 was Orlando+Phoenix+San Diego). Disclosed in normal scope of risk factors.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Concentration is real but properly disclosed. The market-mix drift (Orlando+Phoenix in 2023 → Orlando+Houston in 2024) reflects Scottsdale renovation pulling Phoenix out and is internally consistent with the renovation story. No hidden concentration.

rfm_tuples.R: 'In November 2024, we issued $400 million of 6.625% Senior Notes due 2030 ... and used the net proceeds, together with cash on hand, to redeem in full the outstanding $464.7 million aggregate principal of 6.375% Senior Notes due 2025.' Implicit claim: 2025 wall of maturities refinanced on commercially reasonable terms.
rfm_tuples.f: Cross-check refinancing terms and resulting cost-of-capital signal in EDGAR (8-K terms + 10-K disclosure)
rfm_tuples.M_value: Refinancing confirmed in 10-K Note (Senior Notes) and credit-facility upsizing (8-K 2024-11-12, accession 0001193125-24-256081 and -255204). Coupon on new $400M is 6.625% at par vs 6.375% on retired notes — a 25 bp increase, but only $400M of new vs $465M repaid (so $65M of cash applied to deleverage). Concurrently the corporate credit facility was upsized from $675M to $825M (+$150M revolver/term capacity) and extended to Nov 2028. In Jan 2025 the $100M delayed-draw was funded and used to pay down the $10M revolver and refinance other indebtedness, pushing the next material maturity to 2026 ($55M).
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Refinancing executed pre-cutoff on terms consistent with high-yield BB-tier hotel REIT spreads. 2025 maturity wall ($465M) was eliminated. Cost of capital increased modestly (+25 bp on coupon) but maturity profile improved materially. Implicit 'we can refinance' claim is verified.

rfm_tuples.R: 'Our portfolio of hotels is geographically diverse... primarily in the top 25 lodging markets and key leisure destinations.' AND 'Marriott San Francisco Airport Waterfront' is a 688-room property in CA carrying a $105.97M fixed-rate mortgage at 4.63% due May 2027 (collateralized).
rfm_tuples.f: MODE-B: Identify which of the three mortgaged properties (Grand Bohemian Orlando, Marriott SF Airport, Andaz Napa) is the one with the covenant default. Cross-check disclosure for property-level identification.
rfm_tuples.M_value: The 10-K does NOT explicitly identify which of the three mortgaged hotels is the covenant-defaulted one. By process of elimination and the FY23 framing ('disruption from a significant renovation taking place during the prior trailing 12 months'), the only mortgaged property that underwent a renovation in the relevant TTM is Grand Bohemian Hotel Orlando, Autograph Collection (FF&E work). However Marriott SF Airport Waterfront is also a candidate given SF lodging market weakness post-COVID. The 10-K leaves this ambiguous.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: MODE-B finding: Investors deserve to know WHICH property is in covenant default — a cash trap at the 688-room SF Airport (largest collateral, $106M loan) has different implications than a smaller cash trap at the 248-room Grand Bohemian Orlando ($53M loan). The non-identification is a minor obscurement, especially given the trapped cash now exceeds 5% of cash on hand.

rfm_tuples.R: 'In January 2025, we borrowed the $100 million available on the 2024 Delayed Draw Term Loan and used a portion of the borrowings to repay the full amount outstanding under the Revolving Credit Facility.' (10-K subsequent events; 10-Q confirms.)
rfm_tuples.f: Verify net leverage trajectory — did the company truly delever or just rotate from revolver to term loan?
rfm_tuples.M_value: Per Q1 2025 10-Q debt summary: total debt rose from $1,339M (FY24-end) to $1,438M (Q1'25-end), a +$99M increase, vs only $10M of revolver repaid. Net effect: ~$89M of net new debt added in Q1 2025. Cash applied to fund Q1 2025 share buyback ($35.8M) + $0.14 dividend (~$13M) + escrow cure deposit ($1.5M) + ordinary capex.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: MODE-B finding: The 10-K's January 2025 subsequent-events disclosure frames the delayed-draw as deleveraging-via-refinancing, but in reality net debt increased by ~$89M in Q1 2025 to fund accelerated buybacks. Not deceptive — both events are independently disclosed — but the combined narrative (delayed-draw described as 'repaying revolver and refinancing other indebtedness') downplays that aggregate borrowings rose to fund capital returns. For a 23.6% drawdown name, this is the kind of mild MODE-B fact worth flagging.

summary: Xenia Hotels & Resorts (XHR) discloses a single, lingering mortgage-loan covenant event of default that was first framed in the FY23 10-K (Feb 2024) as a 'renovation-disruption waiver, not an event of default' and has since been re-characterized as an actual event of default cured by $5.0M in cumulative escrow deposits — a real but modest MODE-B claim-drift finding. Beyond that, the disclosure profile is clean: KPMG Big-4 auditor with unqualified opinion (single CAM on hold-period impairment judgment, no impairment taken), no going-concern language, zero insider open-market sales across 25 Form 4s in the trailing 12 months, dividend raised three times through the drawdown ($0.10 → $0.14), share buyback accelerated 4x QoQ ($35.8M in Q1'25 alone), 2025 maturity wall fully refinanced ahead of cutoff at +25 bp coupon, Q1'25 RevPAR +6.7% vs industry +2.2%, and the Grand Hyatt Scottsdale renovation transitioned from FY24 drag to Q1'25 contributor. Two minor MODE-B underdelivery flags (non-identification of which mortgaged property is in default; net debt rose ~$89M in Q1'25 while the subsequent-events note framed the delayed-draw as a revolver paydown). Verdict: this is a healthy boring-middle REIT whose drawdown likely reflects sector-wide concerns (interest rates, group-travel mix, SF/Houston market softness) rather than disclosure-quality issues — i.e., honestly priced bad-news exposure, not a 'lying' name.
